questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes structured pruning from unstructured pruning in neural networks?
questions.choice_A: Structured pruning removes whole neurons, channels, or blocks to match hardware-friendly sparsity, while unstructured pruning removes individual weights based on criteria like magnitude regardless of their placement.
questions.choice_B: Structured pruning is performed only after training, while unstructured pruning can be performed during training.
questions.choice_C: Structured pruning always leads to higher accuracy than unstructured pruning.
questions.choice_D: Unstructured pruning requires rewriting the model architecture, while structured pruning never does.

questions.question: In the context of low-rank factorization of weight matrices in transformers, what is the primary reason it can reduce inference compute?
questions.choice_A: It eliminates attention mechanisms entirely.
questions.choice_B: It decomposes a large dense matrix into two thinner matrices, reducing the number of multiply-accumulate operations when the rank is much smaller than the original dimension.
questions.choice_C: It prunes all negative weights to zero, reducing sparsity overhead.
questions.choice_D: It increases activation sparsity using ReLU gating.

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes knowledge distillation for compressing large language models?
questions.choice_A: Replacing the student’s optimizer with the teacher’s to inherit training dynamics.
questions.choice_B: Copying the teacher’s weights into a smaller student and fine-tuning only the output layer.
questions.choice_C: Training a smaller student to match the teacher’s softened output distribution and/or intermediate representations, often using a temperature to expose dark knowledge.
questions.choice_D: Quantizing the teacher’s weights to reduce memory footprint during training.

questions.question: What is a common drawback of unstructured magnitude pruning when deployed on general-purpose GPUs or CPUs?
questions.choice_A: It cannot achieve high sparsity levels without catastrophic forgetting.
questions.choice_B: It introduces irregular memory access patterns that limit speedups because dense BLAS kernels are highly optimized whereas sparse kernels suffer from indexing and bandwidth overheads.
questions.choice_C: It increases the number of parameters.
questions.choice_D: It requires retraining from scratch to regain any accuracy.

questions.question: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models with top-k routing, what is the main purpose of the capacity factor?
questions.choice_A: To ensure each expert’s parameters are identical to simplify load balancing.
questions.choice_B: To set a per-expert token budget relative to the expected average load, trading off token dropping versus communication/memory cost.
questions.choice_C: To control the learning rate of the gating network independently from experts.
questions.choice_D: To enforce sparsity in the experts’ weight matrices during training.

questions.question: Which training technique is commonly used to encourage balanced expert utilization in MoE models?
questions.choice_A: Gradient clipping on experts only
questions.choice_B: An auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven routing probabilities or token counts across experts
questions.choice_C: Dropout on the gating logits with probability 0.5
questions.choice_D: Weight decay applied only to the router parameters

questions.question: Why might block-sparse pruning (e.g., pruning in contiguous blocks like 4x4 or 16x16) be preferable to fine-grained unstructured pruning for deployment?
questions.choice_A: Block-sparse pruning guarantees no accuracy loss.
questions.choice_B: Block patterns align with hardware kernels and memory layouts, yielding better throughput from fewer indices and coalesced reads while still reducing compute.
questions.choice_C: Block pruning requires no retraining or fine-tuning.
questions.choice_D: Block pruning removes the need for any specialized libraries.

questions.question: In large-scale MoE training across many devices, which communication primitive often dominates runtime and needs careful optimization?
questions.choice_A: Broadcast of model checkpoints
questions.choice_B: All-reduce of optimizer states
questions.choice_C: All-to-all exchanges of token activations between devices hosting different experts
questions.choice_D: Point-to-point transfers of gradients for embeddings only

questions.question: How does quantization interact with weight sparsity when both are applied to a model?
questions.choice_A: Quantization eliminates the need to store sparsity indices.
questions.choice_B: Sparse quantized formats may require storing both quantized nonzero values and their positions; dequantization and gather/scatter can become bottlenecks without specialized kernels.
questions.choice_C: Sparsity makes quantization unnecessary for memory savings.
questions.choice_D: Quantization always converts sparse matrices to dense for faster compute.

questions.question: What differentiates pruning-aware (or training-aware) approaches from post-training pruning?
questions.choice_A: Pruning-aware methods integrate sparsity-inducing regularizers or schedules during training to shape weight distributions, often reducing recovery cost, whereas post-training pruning removes weights after training and typically requires more fine-tuning.
questions.choice_B: Post-training pruning can only be structured, and pruning-aware can only be unstructured.
questions.choice_C: Pruning-aware approaches never use magnitude-based criteria.
questions.choice_D: Post-training pruning guarantees the same accuracy as the dense model without additional steps.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the “Switch Transformer” routing scheme compared to top-2 gating MoE?
questions.choice_A: It routes each token to all experts to maximize capacity utilization.
questions.choice_B: It routes each token to a single expert (top-1), simplifying compute and communication, often at the cost of reduced representational diversity versus top-2.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the gating network and picks experts uniformly at random.
questions.choice_D: It runs a local expert per token to avoid any communication.

questions.question: In practice, why can low-rank adapters (e.g., LoRA) be more attractive than full low-rank factorization for model compression in production settings?
questions.choice_A: They completely remove the base model parameters.
questions.choice_B: They add small low-rank update matrices on top of frozen base weights, enabling task adaptation with minimal additional memory and without retraining the full model.
questions.choice_C: They guarantee faster inference in every deployment scenario.
questions.choice_D: They require no hyperparameter tuning.

questions.question: What is a common risk when distilling a student from a teacher trained with a different tokenizer or pretraining distribution?
questions.choice_A: The student’s training loss cannot be computed.
questions.choice_B: The student may overfit due to having too many parameters.
questions.choice_C: Distributional and vocabulary mismatch can reduce the usefulness of teacher signals, requiring careful data curation, temperature tuning, or intermediate feature distillation.
questions.choice_D: The teacher’s logits become uniformly random and uninformative.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical systems trade-off when choosing a higher MoE capacity factor to avoid token dropping?
questions.choice_A: Lower peak memory due to fewer tokens per expert
questions.choice_B: Reduced communication because fewer tokens are routed overall
questions.choice_C: Increased activation memory and larger all-to-all payloads, potentially lowering throughput
questions.choice_D: Less imbalance because experts receive fewer tokens overall

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of sparsity-inducing regularizers such as L1 penalties or group lasso in training?
questions.choice_A: To ensure gradients are always positive.
questions.choice_B: To encourage weight pruning by pushing individual weights or groups (channels, heads) toward zero, enabling both unstructured and structured sparsity.
questions.choice_C: To increase the margin between classes.
questions.choice_D: To stabilize batch normalization statistics.

questions.question: Why is N:M structured sparsity (e.g., 2:4 on some GPUs) attractive for accelerators?
questions.choice_A: It enforces exactly M zeros per N weights locally, allowing specialized hardware to skip fixed patterns of compute and achieve speedups with limited indexing overhead.
questions.choice_B: It maximizes accuracy at a given parameter count.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for any retraining after pruning.
questions.choice_D: It reduces communication in model parallel training.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the memory footprint of MoE models relative to dense models with the same FLOPs per token at inference?
questions.choice_A: MoE models always use less memory because only a few experts are active.
questions.choice_B: MoE models can have higher parameter memory since all experts must be stored, even if only a subset is activated per token; activation memory may be similar or lower depending on routing.
questions.choice_C: MoE models require no optimizer states during training.
questions.choice_D: MoE models store experts off-device without penalty.

questions.question: When combining quantization with pruning, which practice most reliably preserves accuracy?
questions.choice_A: Prune to the target sparsity and then quantize without any further training.
questions.choice_B: Quantize first, then prune, because quantization reduces the need for sparsity.
questions.choice_C: Use joint or sequential training-aware procedures (e.g., prune with sparsity regularizers and perform quantization-aware training) to adapt the model to both sources of error.
questions.choice_D: Apply per-tensor 1-bit quantization to all layers to avoid bias.

questions.question: What is a key difference between movement pruning and simple magnitude pruning?
questions.choice_A: Movement pruning selects weights to prune based on the direction and consistency of gradient updates over training, whereas magnitude pruning considers only current absolute weight values.
questions.choice_B: Movement pruning is only applicable to convolutional networks.
questions.choice_C: Magnitude pruning requires second-order information.
questions.choice_D: Movement pruning does not require any training signals.

questions.question: In distributed MoE training, how does expert parallelism typically interact with data and tensor parallelism?
questions.choice_A: Expert parallelism replaces the need for data parallelism.
questions.choice_B: Experts are sharded across devices; tokens are routed via all-to-all to the owning devices (expert parallelism), while tensor parallelism shards large matrix multiplies and data parallelism replicates expert shards across groups for throughput.
questions.choice_C: Tensor parallelism is unnecessary when using MoE.
questions.choice_D: Data parallelism handles all routing without communication.

questions.question: Which consideration is most important for achieving actual wall-clock speedups with sparse quantized weights at inference time?
questions.choice_A: Using the smallest possible quantization bit-width regardless of hardware support
questions.choice_B: Ensuring that kernel implementations exploit both sparsity patterns and low-bit arithmetic efficiently, with layouts (e.g., CSR/CSC or block formats) that minimize dequantization and indexing overhead on the target hardware
questions.choice_C: Maximizing the number of experts in the model
questions.choice_D: Avoiding any use of caching during decoding
